title: R
subtitle: The language of statistics and data analysis: vectors, data frames, functions and the native pipe, statistical models, plots, packages and reproducible reports.
description: R is a free, open-source language and environment for statistics, data analysis and graphics. It was created by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland, first announced in 1993, and is modelled on the S language developed at Bell Laboratories. Today it is maintained by the R Core Team and used by statisticians, epidemiologists, biologists, economists, social scientists and data analysts all over the world, with more than twenty thousand contributed packages on [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/) and thousands more for genomics on Bioconductor. Its signature ideas are that every value is a vector, that most operations work on whole vectors at once, and that statistical models are described with formulas such as `weight ~ height`.

This course is for people who can already program a little: if you know what a variable, a loop and a function are (the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience), you are ready. Some familiarity with averages and graphs helps; the statistics are explained as they appear. The course teaches base R, the language as it comes with every installation, and shows how the popular tidyverse packages such as dplyr and ggplot2 express the same ideas, so that you can read and write both.

To run the code yourself, install R from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/) (there are installers for Windows, macOS and Linux) and, if you like, an editor such as RStudio or Positron from Posit. R has no official online playground, but the open-source project [webR](https://webr.r-wasm.org/latest/) runs R in your browser. Every program marked as checked was run by Lumenary's test suite with `Rscript --vanilla` and R 4.1 using only the packages that come with R, and the output shown is the output it printed; everything shown also works in the current release series, R 4.6. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.summary: Where R came from and how to run it, then the building blocks of every analysis: vectors and vectorised arithmetic, indexing, types, missing values and factors, lists and data frames.

levels.title: Practice
levels.summary: Writing functions, control flow, the apply family and the native pipe; reading, reshaping and summarising real data; and fitting and interpreting statistical models with t.test, lm and glm.

levels.title: Professional
levels.summary: Plots with base graphics and ggplot2, packages and CRAN, reproducible environments and reports with R Markdown and Quarto, the tidyverse, testing, and a complete analysis from raw data to report.
